context_question: What are the primary scientific and operational goals this system must achieve for your users, and how will you judge whether it is successful?
answer:
The main scientific goal is to let researchers combine weather observations with ecosystem models so they can run grid-based biogeochemical simulations more efficiently and with less manual effort. Operationally, it needs to hide the complexity of the distributed computing resources, manage inputs and outputs cleanly, and give users a reliable interface for submitting runs and reviewing results.
We’d judge success by whether scientists can get through a full modeling workflow without needing IT support, whether jobs run reliably on the remote resources, and whether the results are easy to visualize and reuse. If it reduces turnaround time for analyses and people trust the outputs enough to use them in their research, that would be a strong sign it’s working.

context_question: Who are the different user and support roles that will interact with this system, and what responsibilities or permissions should each role have across data management, job submission, monitoring, and results review?
answer:
The primary users are the scientific modelers, and they should be able to upload and organize input data, configure and submit modeling runs, monitor job status, and review outputs and visualizations. I’d also expect a smaller group of technical support or system administrators who can manage accounts, resource access, and the grid-side configuration, but they shouldn’t need to touch the scientists’ modeling details unless there’s a support issue.
For permissions, scientists should control their own projects and data, while admins should have broader operational access for troubleshooting, queue management, and system health. There may also be read-only collaborators or reviewers who can view selected results without being able to change inputs or launch jobs, but that would depend on how the research groups want to collaborate.

context_question: For read-only collaborators or reviewers, what exactly should determine which results they can see, and what are the rules for sharing them—for example, is access granted per project, per result set, per run, or by some explicit approval or invitation process?
answer: My expectation is that access would be granted explicitly, not automatically just because someone is in the same organization. The safest default would be per project, with the project owner able to share either the whole project or specific runs and result sets when there’s a reason to do that. I’d also want an invitation or approval step so we can track who can see what, especially if the data are still in progress or not meant for wider distribution.

People gather weather observations and other input files from separate sources, then prepare them locally, submit jobs to remote resources with some technical help, and later pull results back for viewing in separate plotting or analysis tools. It works, but it’s tedious and easy to make mistakes, especially when moving data between steps.

context_question: What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what are the main features you hope to get from this project?
answer: We want to streamline the whole workflow so scientists can manage inputs, run the weather interpolation and ecosystem simulations, and review outputs from one place. The biggest improvement is making remote computing feel transparent and reliable, so users do not need to understand or manually handle the grid environment. We also want better organization of generated outputs so results are easier to find, compare, and reuse.

Are there any other features you would like to see in this project?
answer: Yes, visualization is important, not just basic result viewing. We would also want the system to support checking job status, handling failures clearly, and giving users enough control to rerun or adjust jobs without starting over from scratch. Beyond that, I think the team would also value some way to keep track of metadata so results are traceable back to the inputs and model settings used.

context_question: Based on your description, do you think secure user authentication and access control should also be included so different scientists and support staff can only access the projects, jobs, and outputs they are permitted to use?
answer: Yes, definitely. We need that, especially if multiple research groups are using the same environment and some data or outputs are sensitive or not yet public. Different users should only see the projects and jobs they’re allowed to access, and support staff may need broader rights than regular scientists.

answer: At the top would be secure access and a simple way to manage input data, because nothing else works well without that foundation. Next I’d put running the interpolation and ecosystem simulations through the interface, along with clear job monitoring and failure handling. After that comes results visualization and organized output management, and then the metadata and traceability features.

answer: It should let users bring in weather observations and other model inputs, store them in a consistent place, and keep them organized by project or experiment. Ideally the system would help validate that the files are complete and in the right format before a run starts, so users catch problems early. It would also be useful if inputs could be reused across runs instead of being recopied or re-prepared every time.

answer: I don’t know the exact file types and field rules offhand, because those depend on the specific model setup and the data source we’re using. In general, though, we’d want the system to check that the expected observations are present, timestamps line up correctly, and the files aren’t corrupted or obviously malformed. context_question: Could you describe the current system or process you use to verify input files before a run starts?
answer: Right now it’s mostly a manual process. If something is wrong, they usually only find out after the job fails or the outputs look off, so there’s a lot of wasted time.

answer: Simulation and job execution would be the best next topic. That’s the core of the system, and it ties directly to how users will actually run the models and use the remote resources.

context_question: Please elaborate on what you want the simulation and job execution feature to accomplish.
answer: It should let a scientist configure a run, submit it to the remote computing resources, and then monitor its progress without dealing with the grid infrastructure directly. They should be able to see whether a job is queued, running, failed, or finished, and get a clear reason if something goes wrong. It would also help if they could rerun a job with adjusted settings or use a previous run as a starting point.

context_question: Could you describe how much control users should have when configuring a run, such as which parameters they can change themselves versus which settings should be fixed or managed by support staff?
answer: Users should be able to change the scientific inputs and the main run settings, like which dataset to use, the time range, the spatial region, and the simulation options that affect the experiment. The infrastructure details, job scheduling rules, and resource allocation should be hidden from them and managed by the system or support staff. If there are dangerous settings that could break a run, those should probably be locked down or at least restricted to advanced users.

context_question: To summarize, we’ve discussed secure access, input data management, simulation and job execution, job monitoring and failure handling, visualization, organized outputs, and metadata/traceability. Is there anything else you would like to add?
answer: One thing I’d add is collaboration support, so multiple scientists can share projects, reuse inputs and outputs, and understand who ran what and when. It would also be helpful to have notifications when a run finishes or fails, instead of forcing people to keep checking the system. Beyond that, I think the main functional areas are covered.

context_question: Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?
answer: The main people are the scientists who run the models, because they know the data and workflow best. We should also involve the support or system administrators, since they’ll be responsible for keeping the grid resources working and helping users when jobs fail. If there are data managers or project leads, their input matters too because they care about provenance, sharing, and making sure the outputs are trustworthy.

context_question: What would a successful deployment of this system look like for you and the team?
answer: A successful deployment would mean scientists can get a run set up, submit it, and retrieve results without having to understand the grid underneath. Jobs should run reliably, failures should be understandable, and the outputs should be easy to find, visualize, and share. For the team, it would also mean less manual support work and better confidence that the data and results are traceable.

context_question: To summarize, we discussed secure access, input data management with validation and reuse, simulation/job execution on remote resources with status and failure handling, visualization and organized output management, metadata and traceability, collaboration support, and notifications. Is there anything else you would like to add?
answer: I think that covers the main needs. The only thing I’d emphasize is that the system should stay simple enough for non-technical scientists to use, because if it feels too complex, they won’t adopt it.

We’d need strong authentication, preferably integrated with the institution’s identity system if possible, and all connections to remote resources should be secured so credentials and data aren’t exposed. answer: The most critical qualities are reliability, security, and scientific reproducibility, with scalability also important because runs can be large and compute-intensive. answer: We’d want scientists to become productive pretty quickly, ideally after a short orientation rather than a long technical training cycle. answer: Yes, I think a step-by-step wizard for the main workflow would help a lot, especially if it keeps the user focused on scientific choices instead of infrastructure details. context_question: You’ve highlighted reliability and security as key priorities, which is great. answer: Interrupted transfers should resume from where they left off rather than forcing users to start over, since datasets can be large. For job failures, the system should preserve the job history, capture a clear failure reason, and let users rerun with the same inputs or corrected settings without rebuilding everything manually. Paused sessions are less critical than protecting submitted work, but users should be able to come back later and find their drafts, queued jobs, and results exactly as they left them.

context_question: Thanks for sharing those details on interrupted transfers and job failure handling. answer: One complex case is when a distributed compute node finishes a job but the result never makes it back cleanly, so we’d need the system to detect that uncertainty and avoid presenting incomplete output as valid. Another is inconsistent input versions, where a run starts with one dataset revision and then someone updates or replaces it during processing, so the system should lock or snapshot inputs for the duration of the job. If a remote service or storage target is unavailable, I’d want the system to fail safely, preserve all artifacts it already has, and make it obvious what was completed versus what still needs recovery.

context_question: Building on the reliability and fault tolerance aspects you described, how do you envision the system scaling over time to accommodate increasing numbers of users or larger, more compute-intensive simulation workloads without impacting reliability or the user experience?
answer: I’d expect it to scale mainly by queuing and distributing jobs across more remote resources as demand grows, while keeping the user interface responsive even when the back end is busy. For larger workloads, the system should manage resource limits transparently, so users see accurate progress and estimated wait times rather than timeouts or confusing failures. Reliability should stay intact by isolating jobs from each other, monitoring resource health, and making sure one heavy simulation doesn’t degrade everyone else’s experience.

answer: I’d want the system to scale in a way that’s mostly invisible to scientists, with more back-end capacity added behind the scenes rather than forcing users to change how they work. Reliability would come from strong job isolation, good monitoring, and graceful degradation so a spike in demand slows queued work without breaking active sessions or corrupting results. From the user’s perspective, the important thing is that the interface stays fast, the status information stays accurate, and long-running jobs remain recoverable even under heavier load.

answer: Reliability and data integrity would come first for me, because if users can’t trust the runs and outputs, the rest doesn’t matter much. I’d be more willing to accept a less polished interface or some queueing delays early on than to accept unstable jobs or unclear results.

answer: I’d expect issues like different file layouts, unit mismatches, missing metadata, and older dataset versions that don’t map cleanly to current simulation inputs. context_question: Given how important reliability and data integrity are to you, how would you want the system to handle tricky fault scenarios—like if a job finishes but the results don’t return completely, or if input datasets change during a run? Also, what should happen if remote services or storage become unavailable mid-process to keep scientific accuracy and user trust intact?
answer: If a job finishes but results come back incomplete, I’d want that treated as a failed or incomplete run, not a success, and the user should get a clear explanation with enough detail to decide whether to rerun it. If input data changes during execution, the system should lock or snapshot the version used so the run is tied to a fixed, auditable dataset. When remote services or storage go down mid-process, the job should pause or fail safely, preserve whatever intermediate state exists, and never pretend the output is final until every required piece is verified.

context_question: You’ve emphasized the importance of conservative and traceable corrections during data validation and migration. Could you describe what kinds of traceability or audit features you’d want the system to provide so users can clearly see what was changed, why, and when? How should these features support user confidence and scientific integrity throughout the process?
answer: I’d want a full audit trail for every dataset and job, showing the original input, any conversions applied, who initiated them, the time they happened, and the exact software version involved. It should also keep a clear record of validation warnings, rejected fields, and any manual overrides so users can reconstruct the full chain of custody later. That kind of traceability builds confidence because scientists can verify the provenance of results instead of just trusting the system’s output.

context_question: Given the critical importance you place on reliability and data integrity, how should the system handle complex fault scenarios such as incomplete or partial results, input dataset version locking during runs, or failures in remote services to ensure scientific accuracy and maintain user trust?
answer: I’d want the system to be strict about completeness: if any required part of a result set is missing, the run should stay marked incomplete and never be presented as final. For version locking, the system should freeze the exact dataset snapshot at job start and record that snapshot ID in the output metadata so later changes don’t affect reproducibility. If remote services fail, it should retry only where it’s safe, otherwise fail cleanly, preserve the job state, and give a clear explanation of what happened and what needs to be rerun.

context_question: You’ve shared great detail about handling incomplete results and dataset locking. Building on that, how would you want the system to record and display validation warnings, rejected fields, and any manual overrides so that scientists can easily reconstruct the full chain of custody and confidently verify the provenance of their results?
answer: I’d want those records stored with the run itself and exposed in a readable report tied to the dataset and output products, not hidden in logs that users have to dig for. The display should separate automatic validation issues from manual changes, and every override should show who made it, when, and the reason or comment attached. That way scientists can quickly trace the full history of a result and judge whether it’s acceptable for publication or needs more review.

context_question: How should remote computing resources fit into your overall modeling workflow today, and what does the system need to support from the moment a user wants to use them through getting results back?
answer:
In practice, users should be able to treat remote resources as part of the normal modeling workflow, not as a separate technical step. They would prepare inputs in the system, choose the model run and the available compute target, submit the job, and then monitor progress without having to deal with the grid details themselves.
From submission through completion, the system needs to handle authentication, job staging, transfer of input files, launch and tracking of the run, and retrieval of outputs when it finishes. It should also give users status updates and error messages that make sense to scientists, so they can tell whether a run is queued, running, failed, or ready for review.

context_question: When you think about scientific processing rules and model constraints, what are the main conditions or limits that determine whether a run should proceed as requested, be adjusted in some way, or be stopped and reported back to the user?
answer:
The main thing is whether the inputs are scientifically valid and complete for the model being run. If something is missing or out of range, like incompatible time periods, bad weather coverage, or a grid resolution the model can’t support, then the run should probably be stopped and reported back rather than forced through.
There are also cases where a run could proceed with adjustments, like resampling data to match the grid or interpolating missing weather observations, as long as the system makes that clear to the user. If the issue affects the scientific meaning of the results too much, then I’d want it halted with a plain explanation of what needs to be corrected.

context_question: When users run models and review the results, what do they expect in terms of speed or responsiveness from the modeling and visualization parts of the system, and where do those expectations matter most in their workflow?
answer:
Users expect the interface to stay responsive even when the actual computation takes a long time on remote resources. The most important place for speed is in the day-to-day interaction, like loading data, setting up runs, checking status, and turning results into maps or charts, because that’s where people are actively making decisions.
The modeling itself can take minutes or hours as long as the user gets clear progress updates, and the visualization should render quickly enough to let them inspect outputs without waiting too long between changes. If something is slower, it’s more acceptable in the background processing than in the parts where they’re exploring results or comparing scenarios.

context_question: What are the main open questions, external dependencies, or project risks that could affect whether this modeling workflow can be delivered and used successfully in practice?
answer:
The biggest unknown for us is how stable and accessible the external grid and computing environment will be, because the system depends on resources we don’t fully control. We also need to confirm what data sources and weather observation feeds are actually available, how reliable they are, and whether we have the right access rights and formats.
Another risk is how much model-specific logic has to be built into the system versus handled by existing tools, since that affects schedule and complexity a lot. I’d also watch for security and user-management issues, because if scientists can’t authenticate cleanly or trust the job submission process, they won’t be able to use it comfortably in practice.

context_question: When scientists are using the graphical workflow, what are the main things they’re trying to accomplish there from start to finish, and how do they expect that experience to fit into their day-to-day work?
answer:
They’re mainly trying to move from raw input data to a defensible model result without having to bounce between a lot of technical tools. In the graphical workflow, they should be able to bring in weather and ecosystem data, set up the interpolation or simulation run, launch it on remote resources, and then inspect the outputs in the same environment.
In day-to-day work, they’ll expect it to save them time and reduce manual handling, especially for repeating runs and comparing scenarios. It doesn’t need to replace their scientific judgment, but it should make the workflow consistent, traceable, and easy enough that they can use it regularly without needing grid expertise.

context_question: Are there any specific accessibility needs for the interface, such as support for keyboard-only use, screen readers, or particular contrast or text-size requirements, that should be built into the graphical workflow?
answer:
Yes, we should assume there are accessibility needs, even if we haven’t fully documented every detail yet. At a minimum, keyboard-only use and reasonable screen reader support should be built in, because some users may not be comfortable relying on a mouse-heavy interface.
We’d also want readable contrast and text that can be scaled without breaking the layout, since scientists may be working long sessions and on different machines. I don’t know that we’ve set formal compliance targets yet, so that would need to be confirmed with the team.

context_question: How much manual grid handling do scientists need to do in the graphical workflow, and are there any cases where they should be able to avoid, simplify, or delegate those grid operations entirely?
answer:
Ideally, they shouldn’t need to handle the grid infrastructure directly at all. The system should hide things like node selection, file staging, and job dispatch so scientists can focus on the model inputs and outputs rather than the distributed computing mechanics.
If there are advanced users or administrators, they might be allowed to choose a target resource or adjust run priorities, but that should be optional. For normal scientific use, the workflow should automate as much of the grid handling as possible and only surface it when something goes wrong or needs a decision.

context_question: What specific input file sets are required for interpolation and simulation runs?
answer:
For interpolation, we definitely need the weather observations and the spatial grid or study area definition, and usually some metadata about time range and stations. For simulation runs, we’d need the interpolated weather fields plus the ecosystem or model parameter files, and probably any initial conditions the model depends on.
I’m not sure yet whether there are additional optional files for calibration, land cover, or scenario settings, so that would need to be checked with the scientific team.

context_question: For interpolation runs, under what conditions would you need to include any additional input files beyond the weather observations, spatial grid or study area definition, and time/station metadata?
answer:
We’d need additional files when the interpolation method depends on more context than just the raw observations. For example, if users want elevation, land cover, or other spatial covariates to improve the interpolation, those would have to be supplied too.
It could also come up when there are site-specific corrections, quality-control flags, or calibration datasets that the scientists want applied before the output is generated.

context_question: What kinds of scientific questions or real-world decisions should this modeling work be able to support, and in which situations would scientists choose one use case over another?
answer:
The main purpose is to help scientists understand how weather and ecosystem conditions affect biogeochemical processes over space and time. In practice, that could support things like comparing scenarios, estimating impacts of changing climate or land use, or interpreting how conditions vary across a study region.
They’d choose one use case over another based on the question they’re asking: interpolation when they need a clean weather surface to feed other work, and simulation when they want to predict ecosystem response or test a scenario. If they’re trying to validate assumptions or compare multiple sites, they may run both in sequence.

context_question: When scientists are deciding whether to use interpolation, simulation, or both in sequence, what roles or responsibilities do they typically have in that workflow, and what assumptions do they need the system to preserve or make explicit for them?
answer:
Typically the scientist is responsible for choosing the study setup, selecting the inputs, and deciding whether the output is meant just to support analysis or to drive a full ecosystem run. They also need to review the results and judge whether the run looks scientifically valid, especially if there are choices about station coverage, spatial extent, or scenario parameters.
The system should preserve assumptions like which interpolation method was used, what data version went in, and what time period or grid was applied, so the work is traceable later. It should also make any defaults or automatic steps explicit, because users will want to know whether a result came from their own settings or from system-chosen values.

context_question: Are there any situations where the system should preserve additional workflow assumptions beyond the interpolation method, data version, time period, grid, and defaults—for example, how a run was configured or what automatic preprocessing was applied—to ensure the result can be traced and reproduced later?
answer:
Yes, definitely. If the system does any automatic preprocessing, filtering, unit conversion, gap filling, station screening, or file transformation, those steps should be recorded too, along with the exact run configuration and any parameter values the user didn’t explicitly set.
We’d also want to preserve which software version ran, what remote resource it used, and any job retries or fallback behavior if those could affect the result. The goal is that someone can look at the record later and understand not just the output, but the full chain of choices that produced it.

context_question: When a user leaves a setting blank or accepts a default in the graphical workflow, how should the system show that choice in the run record so it’s clear which values were user-specified and which were filled in automatically?
answer:
The run record should make that distinction very obvious. If the user entered a value, it should be marked as user-specified; if the system filled it in, it should show the actual value used and label it as a default or automatically selected value.
Ideally the record should also capture what the default was at the time of the run, because that matters if defaults change later. If a setting was left blank and the system inferred something from the input data, that should be called out separately so it’s not confused with an explicit user choice.

context_question: As you think about capacity and scalability for these scientific workloads, what does the business need to handle at normal use, and what kinds of increases in demand or data size would you expect the system to accommodate without slowing the work down?
answer:
At normal use, I’d expect the system to support a handful of scientists running jobs, browsing data, and viewing results at the same time without the interface feeling sluggish. It should handle moderate-sized regional datasets and routine interpolation or simulation runs as part of day-to-day work.
For growth, it should tolerate larger study areas, more stations, longer time periods, and more concurrent jobs without forcing users to manage the grid themselves or wait on the UI unnecessarily. I don’t have exact numeric thresholds yet, but the expectation is that the system should scale as data volumes and usage increase in a research setting.

context_question: As usage grows, are there specific performance boundaries you need to protect—for example, a maximum acceptable wait time for model runs or visualization refreshes, or a point where the system should queue work, warn users, or defer less urgent jobs instead of letting the interface slow down?
answer:
Yes, we’d want the interface to stay responsive even if the jobs themselves take a while. If a run is going to take longer than a short interactive wait, the system should hand it off to the backend, show progress, and let the user keep working instead of freezing up.
For longer queues or heavier loads, it should warn the user that the job is waiting and give a sense of expected delay if possible. I don’t know the exact cutoff times yet, but the important boundary is that the UI must not bog down just because the compute workload is growing.

context_question: Would you like to define the scale-up expectations for this now—such as what larger datasets, added users, or heavier job volumes the system should be able to absorb—or should we record those scalability details as still undecided for the moment?
answer: I think we should record those as still undecided for now. We have the expectation that it needs to scale beyond routine use, but the specific dataset sizes, user counts, and job volumes probably need input from the scientific team and whoever owns the infrastructure.

context_question: When a job is waiting behind other work, what should the system tell the user about its status and expected delay, and are there any conditions where that warning should be shown sooner, later, or not at all?
answer:
The user should see that the job is queued, roughly where it stands in the queue, and an estimate of how long the wait may be if we can provide one. If the estimate is uncertain, it should still say that clearly rather than pretending to know.
We’d want the warning sooner when the queue is growing or the job is likely to take a while, and probably not at all for very short waits where the job starts almost immediately. If the system can’t estimate delay reliably, it should still show status changes and avoid giving a false sense of progress.

context_question: What platform or technology constraints should we note for this solution, such as any required grid environment, operating systems, or deployment platforms that the system must support?
answer:
We definitely need to note that it has to work with the existing grid computing environment the organization already uses, because the users shouldn’t have to interact with that directly. Beyond that, I’m not sure we’ve locked down specific operating systems or deployment platforms yet, so I’d treat those as open until the technical team confirms them.
If there are constraints on browser support for the graphical interface or specific remote compute middleware, those should be captured too once we know them.

context_question: Which parts of each model’s workflow should the system handle itself—for example, selecting the right model, preparing inputs, or translating results—versus relying on the existing tools or the scientists to do manually?
answer:
The system should take care of the repetitive workflow steps that are easy to standardize, like preparing inputs, launching the right interpolation or simulation job, moving data to and from the compute resources, and translating the outputs into something the user can view. The scientist should still choose the modeling task, review parameters, and decide whether the result is scientifically acceptable.
If there are specialized external tools already in use, we’d want to integrate with them rather than replace them completely, but I wouldn’t want users manually handling the grid mechanics or file transfers.

context_question: For the graphical interface, which browsers and any remote compute middleware versions or interfaces must we support, and are there any compatibility limits or exceptions we should account for when connecting to the existing grid environment?
answer:
We haven’t finalized exact browser or middleware versions yet, so I can’t name supported versions confidently. The key requirement is that the graphical interface works in the standard browsers our scientists use and can connect cleanly to the current grid environment without exposing its complexity.
If there are older middleware interfaces or site-specific exceptions, those should be documented as compatibility constraints once we verify them with the infrastructure team.

context_question: Which weather observation datasets should the system support for ingestion and organization in the initial release?
answer:
For the initial release, I don’t think we’ve locked down the exact observation datasets yet. We know it needs to ingest weather observations in a form suitable for interpolation, but the specific sources and formats still need to be confirmed with the science team.
It would be helpful for the system to organize them by site, time range, and variable type, but I’d treat the exact dataset list as undecided for now.

context_question: When the external grid or compute environment is unavailable, unstable, or only partly reachable, what should the system do in practice—retry, queue the job, fail fast with a clear message, or fall back to another resource?
answer:
In practice, it should queue the job if the outage looks temporary and keep retrying in a controlled way, because these runs can be long and we don’t want users to lose work unnecessarily. If the environment is clearly unreachable for a longer period, it should fail cleanly with a clear message and preserve the job state so it can be resubmitted later.
I don’t think we’ve decided on automatic fallback to another resource yet, so I’d treat that as optional unless the infrastructure team says there is a supported alternate grid to use.

context_question: What authentication and access-control rules should apply when scientists submit or manage jobs, and are there any trust or authorization checks that should be enforced before a submission is accepted or executed?
answer:
Scientists should authenticate with their own accounts, and access should be limited so they can only submit, view, and manage the jobs and data they’re authorized to use. Before a submission is accepted or sent to the grid, the system should verify that the user has permission for the selected dataset, model, and compute resource.
If a job is going to run under a shared service account or against a protected remote resource, we should also check whatever project-level or resource-level authorization is required there. I’d expect the system to reject anything that fails those checks rather than letting it get halfway through execution.

context_question: What retention period and archival behavior should apply to scientific data once it is no longer actively in use, and are there any cases where it should be kept longer, archived differently, or deleted instead?
answer:
We haven’t set a firm retention period yet, so that part still needs policy input from the science and data management side. My expectation is that active project data should stay online while it’s still in use, then move to some kind of archive when it becomes inactive rather than being deleted right away.
If there are regulatory, publication, or reproducibility reasons to keep certain outputs longer, those should get special handling, but I don’t know the exact rules yet. I'd avoid automatic deletion unless there’s a clear retention policy and approval process behind it.

context_question: What operational rules should govern moving scientific data from active use into the archive—for example, who can trigger the archival move, what conditions make data eligible, and what special handling should apply to outputs with regulatory, publication, or reproducibility obligations?
answer:
Archival should usually be something a project lead or data steward can trigger, not just any user, and the system should also be able to suggest it when data has been inactive for a while. Data should be eligible once the associated job or project is complete and the results have been reviewed or marked as no longer active.
For outputs tied to publication, compliance, or reproducibility, I’d keep them under a special retention flag so they aren’t archived or purged on the normal schedule, and they may need to remain in a more accessible archive with full provenance. I don’t know yet whether those cases need formal approval before moving, but that would make sense to me.

context_question: What ongoing support or maintenance activities should the system need after go-live—such as handling archive requests, correcting retention decisions, or adapting to new rules for keeping or extending the life of data and outputs?
answer:
After go-live, we should expect some routine admin support for archive requests, restoring data that was archived too early, and correcting retention settings when a project’s status changes. The system should also let administrators update retention rules without having to change the software every time the policy shifts.
If new scientific, publication, or compliance rules come in later, the platform should be able to apply those to existing and future outputs in a controlled way, with auditability so we can see what changed and why.

context_question: When a run’s output is deleted, archived, or superseded, what traceability rules should we keep so users can still see which run produced it, whether it was replaced, and how to find any later or related outputs?
answer:
We should keep the run provenance even if the output itself is deleted or moved to archive, so users can still see the original run ID, inputs, timestamps, and who executed it. If an output is superseded, the system should clearly mark that relationship and point to the newer run or output version.
I’d also want links to related outputs and any archived location or recovery path where applicable, because scientists often need to trace a result back later for comparison or publication.

context_question: Do you want automatic deletion to remain off unless there’s an approved retention policy, or should we record that as an undecided rule for now?
answer: Let’s record automatic deletion as off by default unless there’s an approved retention policy in place. That’s the safer assumption for now, and it fits how I’d expect scientific data to be handled.

context_question: When a deleted or archived output’s provenance is retained, are there any cases where access to the original run details should be limited or hidden—for example by project, role, or retention status?
answer:
Yes, access to the original run details should still follow project and role-based permissions, even if the provenance record is kept. So a user might be able to see that a run existed and that an output was superseded, but not necessarily view all underlying inputs or resource details unless they’re authorized.
If a retention status is involved, I’d expect archived or deleted items to be visible only to people with the right project access or admin rights, with more sensitive run details hidden when needed.

context_question: When a user follows a related output link, what should determine whether they can reach the archived version directly, be shown a recovery path, or be redirected to a newer related output instead?
answer:
It should depend on the user’s permissions and the current state of the data. If they’re authorized and the archived version is still available, they should be able to reach it directly; if it’s not directly accessible, they should at least see a recovery or request path.
If there’s a newer related output, the system should redirect or clearly point them to that version, but still preserve the trail back to the original run so they understand the relationship.

context_question: For the graphical interface, do you want any explicit operating system boundaries to apply to the desktop or browser environments scientists use—such as supporting only certain OS families, allowing older lab machines, or treating nonstandard workstation setups as exceptions?
answer:
We should probably define supported operating system families, rather than trying to support everything, because that will help us keep the environment stable. I’d expect current Windows, macOS, and Linux machines to be the normal target, but older lab machines may need to be treated as best-effort or exception cases if they can still run the required browser or desktop components.
For nonstandard workstation setups, I’d prefer they be treated as exceptions and handled only if they don’t break security or the remote access workflow.

context_question: How much of the connection to remote computing resources do you expect the system itself to manage versus relying on existing tools or infrastructure, and are there any cases where model-specific submission or resource-handling rules must be built into the application?
answer:
The system should manage the user-facing connection and job submission flow, but it should rely on existing grid or cluster infrastructure for the low-level resource handling. In other words, scientists should not have to deal with the underlying middleware directly, but we also don’t want to reinvent that part inside the application.
If certain models or simulations have special submission rules, queue requirements, or data staging steps, those should be built into the application where needed so users can run them correctly without manual workarounds.

context_question: For those models or simulations with special submission, queueing, or data-staging needs, what concrete rules should the system enforce automatically, and what should it do when a job does not meet those requirements?
answer:
Where we know the model-specific requirements, the system should automatically enforce them before submission, like checking required input files, selecting the right queue, and staging any needed data to the remote environment. It should also prevent obvious bad submissions, such as missing parameters or using a queue that can’t support the job type.
If a job does not meet those requirements, I’d want the system to stop it early and tell the user exactly what is missing or incompatible, rather than letting it fail later on the grid.

context_question: When several scientists are using the system at once, what should be the practical limits or warning signs that tell you it is reaching its normal concurrent workload capacity—for example, how many simultaneous users or jobs, or what kinds of dataset sizes and run durations should still feel acceptable before you would expect the experience to slow down?
answer:
I don’t have exact numbers yet, but I’d expect the system to handle a modest group of concurrent scientists without noticeable lag in the interface, even when several jobs are queued or running in the background. The warning signs would be slow data uploads, delayed status updates, long waits to open results, or the GUI becoming sluggish while users are managing projects.
For now I’d treat “acceptable” as enough capacity that normal daily team usage feels responsive, and anything beyond that should at least trigger monitoring or a warning so we know when we’re approaching the limit.

context_question: Are there any cases where a job is allowed to proceed only if it uses a shared service account or accesses a protected remote resource, and if so, what specific project- or resource-level checks should the system perform before accepting that submission?
answer:
Yes, there can be cases where a job has to use a shared service account or reach a protected remote resource, but that should be tightly controlled. Before accepting it, the system should confirm the user is in the right project, has permission for that resource, and that the service account or credential being used is approved for that purpose.
If the submission doesn’t match those checks, it should be rejected up front rather than handed off to the grid. I’d also expect an audit trail so we can see who submitted it and what resource it was meant to use.

context_question: Are there any specific import or export file formats, layouts, or validation rules the interface needs to support, and what should happen if a user tries to bring in or save a file in a format that doesn’t meet those expectations?
answer:
We definitely need support for whatever formats our scientists already use for input data and output exchange, but I don’t have the full list finalized yet. At minimum, the system should validate structure and required fields on import so bad files don’t get into a run, and it should preserve the expected layout when exporting results for downstream analysis.
If a file doesn’t meet the expected format, the interface should reject it with a clear explanation of what failed and, if possible, point out how to fix it rather than silently converting or guessing.

context_question: When do you want the system to compare a run’s results against reference results, and what should it do if the comparison shows a meaningful difference from the expected output?
answer:
We’d want that comparison done after a run finishes, especially for models where we have trusted reference outputs or benchmark cases. It’s useful both for routine checks and for verifying that a new dataset or configuration is behaving as expected.
If the comparison shows a meaningful difference, the system should flag the run clearly and let the scientist inspect the results, but it shouldn’t automatically overwrite or hide the output. For a serious mismatch, I’d want it marked as potentially problematic so it can be reviewed before anyone treats it as valid.

context_question: When you organize observations by site, time range, and variable type, are there any special rules for observations that belong to multiple sites, span overlapping time windows, or include multiple variables in one record?
answer:
Yes, those cases need explicit handling. If one observation belongs to multiple sites, the system should either allow it to be linked to each site or make it clear that it is a shared record, depending on how the scientists want to interpret it.
For overlapping time windows or multi-variable records, I’d expect the system to preserve the original observation and not force a loss of detail. It should warn the user if the same data is being assigned in a way that could create duplicates or ambiguity, so they can resolve it before running a model.

context_question: When the same observation could be linked to multiple sites or overlap in time or variables, what exact rule should the system use to decide whether it is treated as a shared record, counted once per site, or blocked as a duplicate before a model run?
answer:
I don’t think we have one fixed rule agreed yet, but the safest default would be to treat it as a shared record only if it was intentionally assigned to multiple sites and the user confirms that. If it’s just an accidental overlap in time or variable definitions, I’d rather have the system count it once and warn about the ambiguity instead of blocking everything.
I’d only block it as a duplicate when the same observation is clearly entered twice with the same site, time, and variable identity. If the exact business rule is important, we’d need to settle that with the science team.

context_question: What should count as a successful modeling run for the scientists, beyond just completing the interpolation and simulation steps?
answer:
A run should count as successful only if it completes without job failures and produces usable outputs that the scientist can actually review or export. It should also pass whatever basic validation we have on the results, like confirming the expected files were generated and the outputs aren’t obviously incomplete or corrupted.
If the run finishes but the results are missing key pieces, I wouldn’t consider that a true success, even if the compute steps technically ended.

context_question: After a run finishes, when should the system perform the comparison against trusted reference or benchmark results, and what should it do if the differences are meaningful but not severe versus serious enough to make the run questionable?
answer:
It should do that comparison right after the run completes and the outputs are assembled, before the results are presented as fully trusted. If the differences are meaningful but still within a tolerable range, the system should flag them for review but still keep the run available.
If the differences are serious enough to make the run questionable, I’d want it marked as suspect or failed validation, with a clear warning that it shouldn’t be used as a final result until someone checks it.

context_question: When a run has completed, what specific outputs or checks must be present for you to consider it truly successful and safe to trust, and are there any conditions under which it should still be treated as not successful even if the job itself finished cleanly?
answer:
A run should only be trusted if the expected output files are present, the results can be opened or visualized properly, and the comparison or validation checks don’t show any major problems. I’d also want the system to confirm that the input data and run settings used were the intended ones, so we’re not looking at a technically complete but misconfigured run.
Yes, it should still be treated as not successful if the job ended cleanly but produced partial outputs, corrupted files, or results that fail validation. In that case I’d want it clearly marked as incomplete or questionable rather than accepted as a valid scientific result.

context_question: For the simulation run, are there any required input files beyond the interpolated weather fields, ecosystem or model parameter files, and initial conditions—for example calibration, land cover, or scenario-setting files—and if so, under what conditions would they be needed?
answer:
Yes, there can be additional required inputs depending on the model configuration. For some studies we’d need calibration files, land cover or vegetation descriptions, and scenario-setting files if the run is meant to represent a specific management or climate case.
I’d expect those to be required only when the selected model or experiment type calls for them, not for every run. If they’re missing for a configuration that needs them, the system should block the run and tell the user what’s absent.

context_question: For interpolation input file sets, are there any situations where the system should require something beyond the weather observations, spatial grid or study area definition, and basic time range or station metadata, and if so what determines when those extra inputs are needed?
answer:
Yes, sometimes. If the interpolation method needs supporting data like elevation, land surface class, or quality-control flags, then those inputs should be required for that specific workflow. Whether they’re needed should depend on the chosen interpolation algorithm and the user’s study setup, not on every interpolation job by default.
If those extra fields are part of the configured method or the dataset is being interpolated across a complex terrain or special region, then the system should ask for them up front and refuse to start if they’re missing.

context_question: Are there any cases where you would want the system to automate part of the scientific decision-making itself, such as choosing among alternative model setups or run parameters, or should that always remain fully in the scientist’s hands?
answer:
I would not want the system making the scientific choice on its own. It can help by suggesting a reasonable default setup or flagging likely issues, but the final decision on model configuration and run parameters should stay with the scientist.
The only automation I’d be comfortable with is routine stuff like filling in known defaults or reusing a previous setup when the user explicitly asks for it.

context_question: For the cases where you do want the system to help with defaults or reuse a prior setup, what specific conditions should trigger that behavior, and are there any situations where it should refuse to apply a default or prior configuration unless the scientist reviews it first?
answer:
Defaults should kick in only when the user is creating a new run from a standard template or has explicitly chosen to reuse a previous configuration. If the system can clearly detect the same study area, same model family, and same kind of data, then it can prefill the usual parameters to save time.
It should refuse to silently apply a default if the change could affect the science, like switching seasons, grid resolution, calibration settings, or a different scenario. In those cases I’d want the scientist to review and confirm the setup before the run starts.

context_question: When a run is starting from a template or a reused configuration, what conditions should the system check to decide whether it can safely prefill values automatically versus requiring the scientist to review the setup first?
answer:
It can prefill automatically when the template matches the intended model type, study area, and data source, and when the reused settings are still valid for the current time period and grid. I’d also want it to check that any referenced inputs still exist and haven’t been changed in a way that would alter the meaning of the run.
If there’s any mismatch in model version, domain, scenario, or calibration assumptions, then it should stop and ask for review instead of filling everything in quietly.

context_question: When a reused input is being checked, what kinds of changes would you treat as significant enough to block the reuse or force a review—for example, changes to the input data itself, the source, the processing method, or just changes in the file location or name?
answer:
A file move or rename by itself shouldn’t block reuse if it’s clearly the same content and the system can still verify it. What matters more is whether the actual data changed, the source changed, or the processing method changed, because those can affect the scientific meaning of the run.
I’d also treat changes in version, time coverage, spatial coverage, or any quality-control status as significant enough to force a review. If the content is identical but just stored somewhere else, that’s fine as long as the system can trace it reliably.

context_question: When a run is canceled before it finishes, what should happen if the scientist later wants to start again from that same run—should the system restore any saved state automatically, or always require a fresh restart and review?
answer:
If the run was canceled before completion, I would want the system to preserve whatever safe intermediate state it already has, but not automatically continue without the scientist looking at it. The scientist should be able to restart from that saved state if it’s still valid, but they should confirm it first.
If anything important changed since the cancellation, like the input data, scenario, or model version, then it should force a fresh restart rather than quietly restoring the old state.

context_question: What should count as the scientist’s confirmation that a canceled run’s saved state is still valid to restart from, and when should the system instead require a fresh restart rather than letting them resume?
answer:
The confirmation can be as simple as the scientist reviewing the preserved inputs and clicking to resume, but it should only be allowed if the system shows the same run context they originally canceled from. That means same study area, same input set, same model version, and same key parameters.
If any of those have changed, or if the saved state is incomplete or expired, then I’d want the system to require a fresh restart. In that case it should clearly explain what changed so the scientist can decide whether to rebuild the run.

context_question: What should the system do when a scientist tries to submit a job but the external grid or compute environment is unavailable, partially reachable, or returns access errors—should it queue the job, retry automatically, route it to another environment, or fail immediately with a clear explanation?
answer:
If the grid is completely unavailable, I’d want the system to fail the submission immediately with a clear message, but keep the job definition saved so the scientist can try again later. If it’s only partially reachable, then a short automatic retry makes sense, but not endless retries that leave the user wondering.
Routing to another environment could be useful only if the scientist or project has already approved that compute target and the inputs are compatible. For access errors, it should fail fast and explain that it’s a permissions or credentials issue, because that usually needs user action rather than automation.

context_question: Would you like to define now how stable and accessible the external grid or compute environment is expected to be for this project, or should we leave that as an open risk for now?
answer: I’d leave it as an open risk for now. We know we need the system to handle outages and access problems gracefully, but I don’t think we should lock down an availability target until we’ve talked with the grid team and the scientists about what’s realistic.

context_question: When the grid is only partially reachable, what should count as a successful retry versus a failure that should stop and surface a message to the scientist?
answer:
A retry should count as successful only if the system can fully verify connectivity and submit the job cleanly, not just get a partial response from the grid. If it can’t reach the scheduler, can’t authenticate, or gets a timeout after a reasonable number of attempts, that should stop and show a clear failure message.
I’d also treat repeated transient errors within a short window as a failure if the system can’t establish a stable path, because otherwise the scientist is just left waiting.

context_question: When a remote run is handed off to the backend, what should count as the threshold for keeping the UI in the responsive state versus warning the user that the offload is taking unusually long?
answer:
I’d keep the UI in a normal responsive state as long as the handoff is still within the expected submission window and we’ve got a live status update from the backend. Once it goes beyond whatever our normal submission time is for that environment, or we stop getting heartbeat updates, then the UI should warn the user that the offload is taking longer than expected.
I don’t know the exact threshold yet, but I’d want it based on observed behavior in that environment rather than a fixed arbitrary number.

context_question: What availability expectation should we set for the service during periods of heavy scientific workload, and are there any planned maintenance or outage windows where lower availability would be acceptable?
answer:
I wouldn’t set a strict availability commitment yet for heavy workload periods. My expectation is that the service should stay usable and not lose work, even if some operations slow down when there are many runs happening at once.
Planned maintenance windows are acceptable if we can announce them ahead of time and the scientists can see them in the interface. I don’t have a defined outage schedule to give you right now, so that part should probably be confirmed with operations and the research team.

context_question: For the performance of modeling and visualization, are there specific workload conditions where scientists should still be able to keep working normally versus conditions where the interface can slow down, batch updates, or defer rendering until the system catches up?
answer:
Yes, under normal loads the scientists should be able to keep working without noticing much delay, especially for navigation, editing inputs, and basic result viewing. If they’re loading large datasets, running multiple simulations, or rendering dense spatial outputs, then it’s acceptable for the interface to slow down, batch updates, or show a progress state while it catches up.
What we should not do is make the interface feel frozen or lose the scientist’s place. Even when we defer rendering, I’d still want the user to be able to cancel, switch tasks, or continue with other work where possible.

context_question: When the interface is slowing down under a heavy workload, what should happen to in-progress actions and queued updates so scientists can keep control of their work without losing context?
answer:
In-progress actions should keep running unless the scientist explicitly cancels them, and the UI should clearly show that they’re still active. Queued updates should stay in order and be applied once the system catches up, so results don’t appear out of sequence or overwrite newer changes.
If something can’t be applied yet, I’d want the system to preserve it and tell the user what’s pending rather than silently dropping it. The main thing is that scientists should always know what has already happened, what is still waiting, and what they can safely do next.

context_question: What should happen if a scientist is working during a planned maintenance window—should the interface block new submissions, let in-progress work continue, or show a clear warning about which actions will be unavailable until the system is back online?
answer:
During a planned maintenance window, I’d prefer the interface to let in-progress work continue if it can, but block new submissions that depend on the unavailable services. It should show a very clear warning about what is affected, what is still safe to do, and when the service is expected to be back.
If something can’t be guaranteed to complete, the user should know before they start it. I’d rather have the system be conservative there than let people begin a run that will just fail halfway through.

context_question: During a planned maintenance window, what should determine whether a user can start a given action at all versus only continue something already in progress, and how should the interface explain any cases where completion can’t be guaranteed?
answer:
The deciding factor should be whether that action needs a service that is going to be unavailable during maintenance. If it depends on the backend, the grid, or an external data source that’s being taken down, then they shouldn’t be allowed to start it; if it’s just continuing a local review or an already submitted run, that can keep going.
The interface should say plainly that the action may not finish because required services are offline, and it should name the affected part if we know it. I’d want the warning to be specific enough that a scientist can decide whether to wait or save their work and come back later.

context_question: When a scientist imports a file for a run, what kinds of validation failures should cause immediate rejection, and what details should the interface show so they can correct the file without guessing?
answer:
Immediate rejection should happen for things like a missing file, an unreadable or corrupt file, the wrong format, or a file that clearly doesn’t match the expected model inputs. If we can detect required fields, invalid dates, bad coordinates, or incompatible units up front, those should also stop the import right away.
The interface should tell them exactly which file failed, what was wrong with it, and where possible which field or row caused the problem. I’d want the message to be specific enough that they can fix it without having to reload the file a few times and guess.

context_question: When a file passes those basic import checks, what other scientific validation rules or model constraints should the system apply before accepting it for a run?
answer:
After the basic checks, the system should validate that the data makes sense for the specific run, like whether the time range matches the simulation period, the spatial extent matches the grid, and the required variables are present for that model. It should also check for obvious scientific inconsistencies, such as impossible values, gaps that are too large for interpolation, or units that don’t line up with the expected inputs.
If a file is technically valid but not suitable for a particular model configuration, I’d still want that flagged before the run starts. The goal is to prevent scientists from launching something that looks fine structurally but will produce meaningless results.

context_question: When the interface connects to the existing grid environment, are there any older middleware paths or site-specific connection behaviors that need to be supported during rollout, and if so, how should the system recognize and handle them without exposing extra complexity to scientists?
answer:
Yes, in practice we probably do need to support some older middleware paths and a few site-specific connection behaviors during rollout, because different labs may still be on slightly different grid setups. The system should recognize those based on configured site profiles or connection metadata, not by asking the scientist to choose technical middleware details.
From the user’s perspective it should just connect successfully or fail with a simple, understandable message if that site isn’t supported yet. If there’s a fallback path, I’d want that handled automatically behind the scenes.

context_question: When a specialized external tool is already part of the workflow, what determines whether we integrate with it as-is, wrap it behind the new system, or treat it as something to be replaced during rollout?
answer:
It should come down to how critical the tool is, how stable its interface is, and how much value we’d gain by keeping it versus replacing it later. If scientists already depend on it and it works reliably, I’d lean toward integrating or wrapping it first so we don’t disrupt their workflow; if it’s brittle, poorly supported, or blocks the new system’s design, then replacement becomes more likely.
We’d also need to consider whether the tool fits the security and distributed-computing setup we’re trying to standardize. If it can’t fit cleanly, I’d rather treat it as a rollout dependency to phase out than force users to manage a messy exception.

context_question: What concrete criteria should determine when a specialized external tool can be kept behind the new system versus when it must be phased out because it cannot meet the standardized security and distributed-computing requirements?
answer:
If the tool can be accessed through a controlled interface, supports our authentication and authorization approach, and doesn’t require scientists to handle grid credentials directly, then I’d say it can stay behind the new system. It also needs to be reliable enough for automated use, and it shouldn’t break our ability to track jobs, data movement, and outputs in a consistent way.
If it can’t meet those basics, or if it forces unsafe workarounds, then it should be phased out. I’d especially be concerned if it can’t run in a way that matches the standardized distributed environment or if it creates security exceptions we can’t justify.

context_question: When a retained external tool doesn’t fully fit the standardized environment, what specific boundary would make it acceptable to use a controlled exception behind the new system, and what would make it unacceptable?
answer:
A controlled exception is acceptable if the tool is isolated behind the new system, only reachable through approved service accounts or wrapped access, and it doesn’t expose extra complexity or credentials to scientists. It also has to be limited in scope so it’s clearly a transitional dependency, not something that weakens the security model for the rest of the platform.
It becomes unacceptable if it requires manual credential handling, direct user access to the grid or host environment, or any workaround that bypasses our audit, authorization, or job control. If we can’t contain the risk and still keep the user experience clean, then I’d say it’s not a workable exception.
